reason: TextMate misreads package references as variables (red) / import paths as strings (green); namespace yellow is the correct meaning and matches One Dark Pro's namespace color
consts are orange by design (constants merged into the literal family, ecosystem-majority ruling 2026-07-20); the Go TextMate grammar cannot see constness
const locals are orange by design (constants merged into the literal family, 2026-07-20); TextMate only marks some declaration sites
enum members are compile-time constants - orange like variable.readonly (constant/literal merge 2026-07-20); TextMate has no enum-member awareness
constructor calls: TextMate guesses function-call blue; semantic class yellow keeps the type family consistent (approved look since Record<> screenshot)
One Dark Pro paints object receivers (variable.other.object) yellow; semantic cannot opt out per-language, and uniform red has been the shipped look since v0.0.2
same as variable: parameters used as object receivers get TextMate receiver-yellow
mid-chain properties (a.b.c) get One Dark Pro receiver-yellow via variable.other.object.property; same decision as variable receivers: identity-consistent red wins

callable parameters invoked directly (callback(x)): TextMate guesses function-call blue; semantic parameter red keeps the variable family (identity principle). TypeScript 7's server classifies by declared type, where the old tsserver reclassified anything in call position as a function
callable variables invoked directly (compilation()): TextMate guesses function-call blue; semantic variable red keeps the variable family. Same TypeScript 7 change as the parameter entry above

function-valued bindings (var assign = require('object-assign')): TextMate sees a variable declaration (red); semantic function blue matches how the same binding is colored in TypeScript files. The binding only gets a function type when TypeScript 7's server has acquired @types for the module (automatic type acquisition), so the token is function or unclassified depending on the environment; both outcomes pass
